stem: A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: Traffic is unpredictable
the table sits idle for hours
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
options.why: [On-demand capacity mode is the better choice](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic) for spiky traffic, and a table [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free) pays no throughput charge in idle hours.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
options.why: Reserved capacity lowers the base price, but auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so sudden spikes are still throttled.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
options.why: With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and the write spikes still reach the table.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.
options.why: Capacity at the peak stops the throttling, but the company pays for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis) in every idle hour.
options.misconception: Provisioning the highest peak around the clock is a cost-effective way to stop throttling.

explanation: For traffic that is idle for hours and then spikes, [on-demand capacity mode is the better choice](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic). The table is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free), so the idle hours cost no throughput. In provisioned mode, auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible) to a sudden spike.
takeaway: Spiky, unpredictable DynamoDB traffic with idle hours: on-demand capacity mode, billed per request.
twin: If the stem said "Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock." instead: provisioned mode with reserved capacity, because it fits a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage).
say: Spiky traffic with idle hours points to on-demand mode, because it bills per request and needs no capacity plan.

stem: A company runs an order application that writes each new order to an Amazon DynamoDB table with a PutItem request. Right after each write, the application reads the same order back with a GetItem request to show a confirmation page. Sometimes the confirmation page shows the previous version of the order. Every read-back must return the result of all earlier successful writes. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: shows the previous version of the order
must return the result of all earlier successful writes

options.text: Read the order back from a global secondary index on the order ID, with a strongly consistent query on the index.
options.why: Queries on a global secondary index [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi), so a strongly consistent query on the index is not possible.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, and send only the GetItem read-back requests through the DAX client.
options.why: DAX serves [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency), and writes that bypass DAX leave the cache to [hold inconsistent values for the same key](../facts/dax.md#dax-bypass-causes-inconsistent-values).
options.misconception: A read from an in-memory cache returns the newest write.

options.text: Set the ConsistentRead parameter to true on the GetItem request that the application sends after each write.
options.why: With ConsistentRead set to true, GetItem returns the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter), which reflects every earlier successful write.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table, and read the newest version of the order from the stream after the write.
options.why: A stream serves other consumers of changes, and [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual), so the read can still miss the write.
options.misconception: A DynamoDB stream returns the newest committed version of an item.

explanation: [Eventually consistent is the default](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-default) for reads, and such a read [might not reflect the results](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-may-lag) of a recent write. A GetItem request with ConsistentRead set to true returns the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter).
takeaway: To read your own write in DynamoDB, set ConsistentRead to true on the table read.
twin: If the stem said "the page can show an order that is a few seconds old" instead: keep the default eventually consistent read, at [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
say: A read right after a write needs ConsistentRead set to true, because the default read is eventually consistent.

stem: A company runs a mission-critical order API on an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every night, a report job scans the whole table with strongly consistent reads and a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN. A small share of the orders are open at any time, and the report can use data that is a few minutes old. During the job, the order API is throttled. Which TWO actions will reduce the read capacity that the job consumes in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN
A small share of the orders are open
the report can use data that is a few minutes old
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Make the filter expression of the scan more selective, so that the scan returns fewer order items to the report job.
options.why: A filter runs after the read, so the scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without it.

options.text: Add an attribute that only open orders carry, create a global secondary index on that attribute, and change the job to query the index.
options.why: The index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key, so it is [faster and less expensive to query that index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan).

options.text: Add a projection expression to the scan, so that DynamoDB returns only the few attributes that the report needs.
options.why: Read capacity depends on [the number of items and the size](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned) of the items that the scan reads, not on the data it returns.

options.text: Change the scan of the report job from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads, and keep the same filter expression.
options.why: Eventually consistent reads cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost), and the report accepts data that is minutes old.

options.text: Copy each open order into a second DynamoDB table with a Lambda function on the stream of the table, and scan the second table.
options.why: The copy shrinks the scan, but the company pays for a second table, every copied write, and Lambda code that the team maintains.
options.misconception: A copy that custom code keeps in sync is the cheapest way to isolate a report.

explanation: A filter does not help, because the scan still [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity). A sparse global secondary index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key attribute, so the job reads far fewer items. Eventually consistent reads then cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
takeaway: Filters and projections do not lower scan capacity; a sparse index and eventually consistent reads do.
twin: If the stem said "the report lists every order, open or closed" instead: the sparse index stops helping, because the job reads every item, and eventually consistent reads still help.
say: To cut the read capacity of a report, I query a sparse index and use eventually consistent reads; a filter saves nothing.

stem: A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Point-in-time recovery is turned on with its default settings, and an on-demand backup of the table is taken every Sunday. The table also has a DynamoDB stream that a search service reads. On Tuesday at 14:05, a faulty release deleted thousands of order items. The team found the problem on Friday. The company must get the deleted items back as they were at 14:04, a point in time before the error. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: as they were at 14:04
The team found the problem on Friday

options.text: Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 directly into the existing table, so that the production table rolls back in place.
options.why: You [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore, so no restore rolls the production table back in place.

options.text: Restore the Sunday on-demand backup to a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.
options.why: The Sunday backup misses the orders that were created or changed between Sunday and Tuesday, so the items do not come back as they were at 14:04.
options.misconception: The latest scheduled backup is good enough for a recovery to an exact time.

options.text: Read the old images of the deleted items from the DynamoDB stream of the table, and write the items back into the production table.
options.why: Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so the records of the Tuesday deletes were removed from the stream before Friday.

options.text: Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 as a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.
options.why: Point-in-time recovery [always restores to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), and copying the deleted items back returns them as they were at 14:04.

explanation: Point-in-time recovery protects a table [from accidental write or delete operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-protects-accidental-writes-deletes). The process [always restores to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), because you [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore. The team restores to 14:04 and copies the deleted items back into production.
takeaway: A DynamoDB point-in-time restore creates a new table; copy the items back or switch the application to it.
twin: If the stem said "a faulty release deleted the whole table" instead: restore the [system backup](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-deleted-table-system-backup) that DynamoDB creates when a table with point-in-time recovery is deleted.
say: Point-in-time recovery restores into a new table, so I restore to 14:04 and copy the deleted items back.

stem: A startup with a small team is building a serverless backend for a mobile app. AWS Lambda functions handle every request. Each request reads or writes one user session by its session ID, and no request joins session data with other data. Traffic swings from almost nothing at night to millions of requests at peak. Session data must be stored durably. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: reads or writes one user session by its session ID
Session data must be stored durably
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a Multi-AZ deployment, with each Lambda invocation opening its own database connection
options.why: Unlike RDS, [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections); a connection per invocation at peak needs pooling, and the team still sizes DB instances.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, with the session ID as the partition key of the session table
options.why: DynamoDB fits [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store), and you [don't need to provision any servers](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-serverless-no-servers); on-demand mode can [handle fluctuating traffic](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic).

options.text: A self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones
options.why: DynamoDB, instead of a self-hosted NoSQL database, [can reduce operational overhead](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-managed-nosql-reduces-overhead); here the team patches and scales the instances.
options.misconception: A NoSQL database on your own instances costs the team about the same effort as a managed one.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache as the only store of the session data, with the session ID as the key of each item
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), so it does not meet the need to store session data durably.

explanation: Each request reads one item by its key, with no joins, which fits a key-value database for [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store). With DynamoDB you [don't need to provision any servers](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-serverless-no-servers). Lambda calls it without connection pools, because [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections).
takeaway: Key-value sessions, spiky traffic and a small team: DynamoDB in on-demand mode.
twin: If the stem said "the app joins sessions with orders in ad hoc SQL reports" instead: a relational database such as Amazon Aurora, because DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator).
say: One session per key, no joins and spiky traffic point to DynamoDB in on-demand mode, with no servers to manage.

stem: A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: Traffic is steady-state and predictable
almost all of its provisioned capacity
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
options.why: At steady, high use, on-demand is not the cheaper mode: it costs less when the average utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization).

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
options.why: Provisioned mode fits a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage), and reserved capacity, bought with a [one-time partial upfront payment](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-reserved-capacity-terms-and-discount), lowers the rate of that load.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
options.why: With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and every write still uses the capacity of the table.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.
options.why: Fixed capacity at the peak pays the standard rate for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis), with no reserved discount.
options.misconception: Turning off auto scaling at the peak level is the cheapest setup for a steady table.

explanation: The table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity all day. An ideal workload for provisioned mode has a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage), and on-demand is cheaper only when utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization). Reserved capacity then lowers the rate of the base load.
takeaway: Steady, predictable DynamoDB traffic near the provisioned level: provisioned mode plus reserved capacity.
twin: If the stem said "Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes." instead: on-demand capacity mode, because it is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free).
say: Steady traffic that fills the provisioned capacity stays in provisioned mode, and reserved capacity lowers the rate.

stem: A company keeps 5 years of order history in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses the DynamoDB Standard table class. The company must retain all of the orders, and the application reads old orders through the same DynamoDB API as new orders. Orders older than one month are infrequently accessed. Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill of the table. The company does not want to change the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: must retain all of the orders
infrequently accessed
Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Enable Time to Live on the order table so that DynamoDB deletes each order item one month after the order date.
options.why: Deleting old orders lowers the bill, but it breaks the requirement to retain all of the orders.

options.text: Export the orders older than one month to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and delete those orders from the table.
options.why: Archived orders leave the table, so the application can no longer read them through the same DynamoDB API.

options.text: Change the table class of the order table from DynamoDB Standard to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.
options.why: Standard-IA has [lower storage costs than DynamoDB Standard](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost), and the switch [does not require changing your application code](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-switch-no-code-change).

options.text: Keep the DynamoDB Standard table class, and purchase reserved capacity for the reads and writes that the table uses each month.
options.why: Reserved capacity discounts only reads and writes, but here [storage is the dominant cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost), and Standard-IA lowers it.
options.misconception: A commitment discount on throughput is the biggest saving for every table.

explanation: Storage is about 70% of the bill, and DynamoDB Standard-IA suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or more of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage). It offers the [same performance, durability, and availability](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-same-performance) as Standard, and the switch [does not require changing your application code](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-switch-no-code-change).
takeaway: When storage is half or more of a DynamoDB bill, switch the table class to Standard-IA.
twin: If the stem said "Storage is about 20% of the monthly bill" instead: keep DynamoDB Standard, which suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or less of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage).
say: Storage is most of the bill and old orders are rarely read, so I switch the table to Standard-IA, with no code change.

stem: A company runs a loyalty program that stores the points balance of each user as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table. A transfer moves points from one user to another. The transfer is transactional: the debit of one item and the credit of the other item must both succeed or both fail, and the debit must fail if the balance is too low. Clients sometimes time out and send the same transfer request again. The company must ensure that no transfer is applied twice. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: must both succeed or both fail
send the same transfer request again
LEAST development effort

options.text: Send one BatchWriteItem request that holds both balance changes, and send the same request again when the client times out.
options.why: With BatchWriteItem, [only some of the actions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem) might succeed, so a debit can be written without its credit.

options.text: Send two UpdateItem requests that change the balances with atomic counters, and retry each request when the client times out.
options.why: With atomic counters, [the updates are not idempotent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-atomic-counter-not-idempotent): each retry moves the points again, and the two requests can succeed separately.
options.misconception: An atomic counter update can be retried safely.

options.text: Send two conditional UpdateItem requests, store each request ID in a second table, and write code that reverses a failed transfer.
options.why: This design can work, but the team writes and maintains rollback code and duplicate checks that a transaction already provides.
options.misconception: Custom rollback code is the normal way to make two writes succeed or fail together.

options.text: Send one TransactWriteItems request with both updates, a condition on the balance, and a client request token for each transfer.
options.why: TransactWriteItems gives a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing), and the request can [include a client token](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token) so that a repeated request is not applied twice.

explanation: One TransactWriteItems request makes both updates with a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing). A condition on the balance stops a debit that is too large, because [a conditional write succeeds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-conditional-write-succeeds-only-if-condition) only if its condition is met. The client can [include a client token](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token) to make a retried request idempotent.
takeaway: Two items that change together, with safe retries: TransactWriteItems with conditions and a client token.
twin: If the stem said "a client can repeat a request an hour later" instead: also store each request ID and check it in the transaction, because a client token is valid for [10 minutes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transaction-client-token-10-minutes).
say: Both writes succeed or fail together, so I use TransactWriteItems with a condition and a client token for retries.

stem: A company is building a reporting service for its sales team. Every week, analysts write new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products, and the access patterns are not known in advance. The data is relational and changes all day as new orders arrive. The team has two developers and no database administrator. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products
the access patterns are not known in advance
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, with the orders, customers, and products in related tables that the analysts query with SQL
options.why: Aurora fits [less predictable query patterns](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins), and relational databases support [complex queries through joins](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins).

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB, with one table for each entity and a global secondary index for each report that the analysts need
options.why: DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator), and NoSQL data is [queried efficiently in a limited number of ways](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-nosql-queries-efficient-in-limited-ways), not by new ad hoc queries.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache, as the fully managed in-memory store that holds the orders, customers, and products for the reports
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), a layer in front of a database, so it is not the store of record for the reports.

options.text: PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances that the developers install, patch, back up, and scale for the SQL queries of the analysts
options.why: PostgreSQL on EC2 runs the joins, but the two developers patch, back up, and scale the instances themselves.
options.misconception: A database on your own instances gives the same result with the same effort as a managed one.

explanation: The analysts write new joins every week, so the access patterns are not known in advance. The AWS decision guide points to Aurora for [less predictable query patterns](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins). Aurora is a [fully managed relational database engine](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-is-managed-relational-engine), so the two developers do not run database instances themselves.
takeaway: Ad hoc SQL with joins and unknown access patterns: a relational engine such as Aurora, not DynamoDB.
twin: If the stem said "every request reads one order by its order ID, with no joins" instead: Amazon DynamoDB, because for that access AWS says to [consider a NoSQL database such as DynamoDB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-oltp-dynamodb-vs-rds-joins).
say: New joins every week mean unknown access patterns, so I choose Aurora, not DynamoDB.

stem: A web application stores user sessions in an Amazon DynamoDB table that holds millions of items. The application reads each session by its session ID. Each session must expire one hour after its last use, and the application must never accept an expired session. Old session items must be removed from the table automatically. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must never accept an expired session
removed from the table automatically
MOST operationally efficient

options.text: Store the expiry time of each session as a Number in Unix epoch seconds, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
options.why: The TTL attribute uses [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and TTL deletes items [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

options.text: Enable Time to Live on the expiry attribute, and accept every session item that a read returns, because expired items are gone.
options.why: DynamoDB deletes expired items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so a read can still return an expired session.

options.text: In every session read, compare the stored expiry time with the current time, and reject any session item that has expired.
options.why: Expired items [continue to show in read and write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-expired-items-visible-until-deleted) until deletion, so the application checks the expiry time on every read.

options.text: Store the expiry time of each session as an ISO 8601 date string, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
options.why: Items whose TTL attribute is not a Number are [ignored by the TTL process](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored), so the sessions stay in the table.
options.misconception: Time to Live reads any date format.

options.text: Run a Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table and deletes expired session items.
options.why: The job works, but the team maintains code, and its scans and deletes use capacity; TTL deletes [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).
options.misconception: A scheduled clean-up job is the standard way to expire DynamoDB items.

explanation: TTL removes old sessions without code: the expiry is a Number in [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and the deletes run [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput). TTL is not exact: items go [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so every read also rejects an expired session.
takeaway: TTL deletes expired items within days, not at once; reject expired items in every read.
twin: If the stem said "an expired session can be accepted for a few days" instead: TTL alone is enough, because DynamoDB deletes items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu).
say: TTL cleans up expired sessions without write cost, but late, so the application still checks the expiry time on every read.

stem: A company runs applications in private subnets of a VPC and servers in its on-premises data center. The data center connects to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect. Both the applications and the servers read and write items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the same Region. All traffic to DynamoDB must reach the service privately, without using the public internet. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: private subnets of a VPC
servers in its on-premises data center
without using the public internet
MOST cost-effective

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and route the DynamoDB traffic of the private subnets through the NAT gateways.
options.why: A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and NAT gateways charge per gigabyte [regardless of the traffic's source or destination](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-data-processing-any-destination).
options.misconception: Private subnets need a NAT gateway to reach DynamoDB.

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, and add the endpoint to the route tables of the private subnets of the applications.
options.why: A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).

options.text: Route the requests of the data center servers over Direct Connect to the gateway endpoint that the private subnets use.
options.why: Gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks; for that case [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink).

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of the data center servers to it over Direct Connect.
options.why: For on-premises access [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which uses [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of both the applications and the data center servers to it.
options.why: This works, but PrivateLink is [available for an additional cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-vs-privatelink-cost-note), and the applications can use a gateway endpoint instead.

explanation: The two groups of callers need two endpoint types. In the VPC, a gateway endpoint has [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge). Gateway endpoints do not serve the data center, so [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which reaches DynamoDB through [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).
takeaway: VPC callers use the gateway endpoint at no extra charge; data center callers use an interface endpoint.
twin: If the stem said "only the applications in the VPC use the table" instead: the gateway endpoint alone, because there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).
say: Inside the VPC I use the gateway endpoint at no extra charge; from the data center I use an interface endpoint.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for two actions that keep all DynamoDB traffic private at the lowest cost.
I mark the constraints: applications in private subnets, servers in the data center behind Direct Connect, no public internet, and MOST cost-effectively.
Before I look at the options, I predict one interface endpoint for DynamoDB for everything, because PrivateLink serves both the VPC and the data center through private IP addresses.

I remove the NAT gateways, because a gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB without a NAT device and NAT gateways charge for every gigabyte. I remove the data center route to the gateway endpoint, because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks.

Between one interface endpoint for all callers and a gateway endpoint plus an interface endpoint, the difference is cost. My first idea breaks because the applications in the VPC can use a gateway endpoint at no additional charge, and PrivateLink is available for an additional cost.
Check: the gateway endpoint serves the applications at no extra charge, the interface endpoint serves the data center servers, and no request uses the public internet. Time: 90 seconds.
